lead: A flitched beam is a timber beam with steel plates bolted or glued to it so both materials bend as one. Timber is cheap and light; steel is stiff. They share moment in proportion to stiffness. Only a few universities teach this. The tool is the modular ratio: replace steel by m times timber width, find one neutral axis, multiply steel stress by m. It appears in old timber bridges, temporary props and repair work.
prereq: You need: 4.2 for M/I = σ/y, 4.1 for centroid and I, and Unit 1 for modular ratio.

sections.h3: Full composite action and modular ratio

blocks.text: Full composite action means equal curvature 1/R in steel and timber. At distance y from the neutral axis, strain is ε = y/R and stress is σ = Eε, so σ_s = m σ_t, where m=E_s/E_t is the modular ratio, E_s is steel Young's modulus and E_t is timber Young's modulus; m≈20. Moment share follows EI, so stiffness decides share. The transformed section replaces each steel area by m times the timber area; then the ordinary bending formula applies. The neutral axis is the real one. The usual textbook picture is a steel plate on each side of the joist, or one plate clamped between two joists; top-and-bottom plates use the same method, only steel geometry changes. Bolts, nails or glue must prevent slip. Without connectors, steel carries less and timber more than full-composite values: steel stress falls, timber stress rises, deflection increases.

blocks.where: m is the modular ratio; E_s is steel Young's modulus; E_t is timber Young's modulus. m is dimensionless.

items: Take timber as base; find m.
Replace steel width b_s by m b_s; keep thickness.
Compute I_tr=Σ(b_i t_i³/12 + A_i d_i²), where b_i is transformed width, t_i thickness, A_i=b_i t_i, d_i distance from rectangle centre to neutral axis.
Stresses: σ_t=M y/I_tr; σ_s=m M y/I_tr, with y from neutral axis. Use N and mm for MPa. Check timber and steel separately. Since m>1, steel stress is m times timber at same y; do not omit m.

blocks.where: I_tr is the transformed second moment of area; b_i, t_i, A_i and d_i are defined in step 4.

figure.caption: Timber core 100 mm wide, 200 mm deep, with 10 mm steel plate top and bottom. Steel stress is m times timber stress at the same level.

examples.question: Timber core 100 mm × 200 mm; two steel plates 100 mm × 10 mm top and bottom. E_s=200 GPa, E_t=10 GPa, M=30 kN·m. Find max timber and max steel stress.
steps: m=E_s/E_t=200/10=20. Transformed plate width=m b_s=20×100=2000 mm; thickness stays 10 mm.
By symmetry neutral axis is mid-depth. Timber y_max=100 mm. Steel centre y=105 mm; outer steel face y=110 mm.
I_t=100×200³/12=6.667×10⁷ mm⁴. Each plate: I_self=2000×10³/12=1.667×10⁵ mm⁴; A=20000 mm²; A d²=20000×105²=2.205×10⁸ mm⁴; plate total=2.207×10⁸ mm⁴. Two plates=4.413×10⁸ mm⁴. I_tr=5.08×10⁸ mm⁴.
At plate centre: σ_s=(20×30×10⁶×105)/(5.08×10⁸)≈124 MPa. Maximum at outer y=110: σ_s=(20×30×10⁶×110)/(5.08×10⁸)≈130 MPa. Compare 130 MPa with allowable steel stress.
examples.answer: Maximum timber stress 5.91 MPa; maximum steel stress ≈130 MPa at outer face (124 MPa at plate centre); full composite action assumed.
examples.check:
m=int(200/10)
bt=100
ht=200
bs=100
ts=10
M=30e6
It=bt*ht**3/12
ys=ht/2+ts/2
yo=ht/2+ts
Is=2*((m*bs)*ts**3/12+(m*bs*ts)*ys**2)
I=It+Is
st=M*(ht/2)/I
ssc=m*M*ys/I
ssmax=m*M*yo/I
print(m)
print(I)
print(round(st,2))
print(round(ssc))
print(round(ssmax))

traps: Using actual steel width b_s instead of m b_s; steel appears 20 times too weak.
Forgetting m when reporting steel stress; transformed result is timber-equivalent.
Assuming full composite action without checking connectors; slip lowers stiffness and raises timber stress.
Using m=E_t/E_s or mixing GPa with MPa; m is dimensionless.
Taking steel y=100 mm at timber–steel interface instead of 110 mm at outer steel face understates maximum steel stress.

quiz.a: A timber beam with steel plates bolted or glued to it so both bend together.

quiz.q: Define modular ratio and give its value in the worked example.
Why multiply steel width by m in the transformed section?
quiz.a: It converts steel area to equivalent timber area, so one material formula works; width scales by m.

quiz.q: If E_steel=210 GPa and E_timber=7 GPa, find m.
Symmetric flitched beam: timber 80 mm×160 mm, two steel plates 80 mm×8 mm. m=20, M=20 kN·m. Find I_tr and max steel stress.
quiz.a: I_t=80×160³/12=2.73×10⁷ mm⁴. Each transformed plate: I_self=1600×8³/12=6.83×10⁴ mm⁴; A=12800 mm²; A d²=12800×84²=9.03×10⁷ mm⁴. Two plates=1.81×10⁸ mm⁴. I_tr≈2.08×10⁸ mm⁴. At plate centre y=84: σ_s=(20×20×10⁶×84)/(2.08×10⁸)≈161 MPa. Maximum at outer y=88: σ_s=(20×20×10⁶×88)/(2.08×10⁸)≈169 MPa.

quiz.q: If bolts slip, how do steel stress, timber stress and stiffness change?
quiz.a: Full composite action is lost. Steel carries less, so steel stress falls. Timber carries more, so timber stress rises. Stiffness falls, so deflection increases.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern composite steel-concrete beams use shear studs and the same transformed-section idea with modular ratio.
